title: Contextual retrieval and search quality improvements

opening.headline: Diagnose problems where context is lost as chunks fall out of the document, and learn how to restore context to improve search quality.
body: Searching by dividing the document into chunks improves efficiency, but if you read only one chunk, you may not be able to tell which company the story is from and which period. These chunks are hard to find, and even if you do find them, they're hard to use.

In this lesson, we will explore the principles of context search, which is attaching descriptions to chunks. Next, we check hybrid search using embedding and BM25, and re-ranking to re-select candidates step by step, and interpret the results as a measure of how much search failure is reduced when these techniques are accumulated.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the principles of context search techniques
Can diagnose chunk context loss issues

screens.title: Chunks that stand alone and don't know what they're talking about
screens.lead: Read the query and the retrieved chunk side by side. Think about whether you can answer the question by just looking at this chunk.

visual.alt: A scene with a question bubble, a searched chunk card, and two question marks asking which company and which branch.
labels: What is ACME's sales growth rate in the second quarter of 2023?
The company's sales increased by 3% compared to the previous quarter.

paragraphs: The question is, ‘What is ACME’s sales growth rate in the second quarter of 2023?’ The retrieved chunk says, ‘Company sales increased 3% over the previous quarter.’ Although the content appears relevant, this chunk has neither the company name nor the time period. Since you don't know which branch of which company it is, it's hard to determine if it's the right chunk.

Anthropic's context search article explains that traditional RAGs often lose context while encoding information, resulting in relevant information not being found in the knowledge base. This is because the process of dividing a document into small chunks does not increase efficiency, but separates each chunk from its position and background in the original document.

If the chunks are not self-contained, two problems arise: First, it fails to raise the right chunks during the search phase. Second, even if found, it is difficult for the model to accurately write based on that chunk. This lesson covers context retrieval, which brings context back to chunks.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Would this problem go away if I split it into larger chunks? Continue class by thinking about ways other than increasing the size.

screens.outro: First, let me recall your experience.

screens.title: Thinking about meaningless chunks in isolation
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think of it first and then press it.

items.prompt: Are there cases where you don't know what the searched chunk means on its own?
items.answer: Representative examples include chunks that start with a pronoun or presuppose the preceding paragraph, and chunks in which only part of the table is cut out. Even if a human reads these chunks, it is difficult to know which part of the document it is.

items.prompt: What was the model’s answer then?
items.answer: The model can take chunks without context and still come up with a plausible answer. Typical errors include mixing figures from different companies or quarters, and these errors are more dangerous because they are not apparent.

items.prompt: Are there any methods you have tried other than changing the chunk size?
items.answer: There are many cases where you have used the method of attaching the document title to the front of the chunk or adding a document summary. Anthropic reports that they tried chunking a general summary of the entire document, but the benefit was very limited. The starting point of this class is that each chunk requires an explanation appropriate for that chunk.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's take a closer look at the process of attaching context to chunks.

screens.title: The process of attaching context descriptions to chunks
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the original chunk and the context-laden chunk are treated differently in the search.

visual.alt: The processing flow is to give the entire document and chunk to Claude to create a context description, prepend it to the chunk, and write it to the embedding and BM25 index.

states.label: original chunk
states.body:
**Chunk Content**: 'Company sales increased 3% over the previous quarter.'

**Appearance in Search**: The embedding for this chunk contains no information about which company it is or which time period it is from. Compared to the query 'ACME's sales growth rate in the second quarter of 2023', the topic of sales growth rate is close, but it is not clear whether the company and period are correct. Similar chunks from different companies compete in the same rankings.

**Appearance in BM25**: The word 'ACME' is not in the chunk and cannot be found by lexical matching.

**Result**: Either the correct chunk doesn't make it to the top, or if it does, the model isn't sure which company it belongs to.

states.label: Add context
states.body:
**How to make it**: Context retrieval gives Claude an entire document and a chunk, and has him create a short context that describes this chunk within the entire document. The request text states that you only reply with concise context to improve search. The attached description is usually 50 to 100 tokens.

**Example of attached chunk**: 'This is from ACME's SEC disclosure for the second quarter of 2023, and sales in the previous quarter were $314 million. The company's sales increased by 3% compared to the previous quarter.'

**Appearance in Search**: This description is prepended to the chunk before creating the embedding and before creating the BM25 index. So both semantic search and lexical search get to know the company and the period.

**Cost**: Prompt caching saves you from having to read the document repeatedly in chunks. Anthropic calculates that the one-time cost in this case is $1.02 per million document tokens.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the effectiveness, let's look at a hybrid search that combines semantic search and lexical search to identify candidates.

screens.title: Hybrid search and re-ranking
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to see step by step the process by which candidates are filtered out after an inquiry is received. Notice how the number of candidates decreases.

visual.alt: A funnel-shaped pipeline that merges the embedding and BM25 search results and re-ranks them, leaving only the top 20.

steps.title: Step 1: Embedding search captures meaning
steps.body: Embed the query to find chunks with close meaning. It is strong in finding chunks with the same meaning even if the expressions are different. On the other hand, Anthropic's article points out that embeddings can miss items that should match exactly.

steps.title: Step 2: BM25 search catches the exact word
steps.body: BM25 uses vocabulary matching to find exact word or phrase matches. It is especially effective for queries containing unique identifiers or technical terms. For example, when searching for 'Error code TS-999', it finds documents with exactly that string.

steps.title: Step 3: Merge the two results
steps.body: The top results from both methods are combined using a rank merge technique and duplicates are removed. This ensures both accurate term matching and broad understanding of the meaning. In Anthropic's experiment, the method that used both embedding and BM25 was better than the method that used embedding alone.

steps.title: Step 4: Re-rank many candidates
steps.body: In a large knowledge base, an initial search may return hundreds of chunks of varying relevance. Re-ranking puts each candidate into a re-ranking model along with a query, re-evaluates them by relevance and importance, and only the top few remain. In our experiment, we picked the top 20 out of 150 initial candidates.

steps.title: Step 5: Enter 20 into the prompt
steps.body: The 20 selected chunks are put into the prompt to generate an answer. Anthropic reports that 20 doses were more effective than 5 or 10. Re-ranking reduces the amount of processing the model needs to do, thereby improving response quality while reducing cost and delay.

steps.title: Step 6: Consider the cost
steps.body: Re-ranking adds one step to execution time, which introduces some delay and costs money. There is a trade-off where re-ranking more candidates increases performance, but also increases delay and cost. The documentation recommends experimenting with different settings for your use case to find a balance.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified each technique, let's interpret the cumulative effect of these techniques in terms of measurements.

screens.title: Commentary: Effects of combining embeddings, BM25, and reranking
screens.lead: Move the sliders to add techniques one by one. You can see with the instructor's interpretation how the rate of search failures within the top 20 is reduced.

visual.alt: Four bar graphs showing the search failure rate decreasing from 5.7% to 1.9% as techniques are added.

stops.body: In an experiment averaging multiple knowledge domains, when only general embeddings were used, the rate of not finding relevant documents within the top 20 chunks was 5.7%. This value is the baseline. Anthropic measured failure as 1 minus recall@20. All subsequent values ​​are reductions compared to this baseline.

When we embedded the chunks with context descriptions, the failure rate went down to 3.7%. That's a reduction from 5.7% to 3.7%, which the document describes as a 35% reduction. As the chunks became self-contained, the accuracy of semantic retrieval increased.

When we also created a BM25 index with context-attached chunks and used it with embedding, the failure rate was 2.9%. This is a decrease of 49% from 5.7%. It can be interpreted that embedding, which captures meaning, and BM25, which captures accurate words, filled each other's weaknesses.

Adding re-ranking, the failure rate dropped to 1.9%, a 67% reduction. The document summarizes that all of these benefits are stacked. Combining the 20 chunks of contextualized embedding, contextualized BM25, reranking, and prompting gave the highest performance.

These values are experimental results averaged over multiple areas, so it is not guaranteed that our data will have the same width. The documentation encourages you to experiment directly with chunk boundaries, embedding models, and number of chunks, and emphasizes that you should always run evaluations. It should also be noted that re-ranking is a step that increases delays and costs.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the size of the effect, we will summarize the lesson in the final screen.

screens.title: Search quality starts with chunk context
screens.lead: The first question, what to do when a chunk loses context, is answered with what we learned today.

paragraphs: The first chunk I saw, 'Company sales increased by 3% compared to the previous quarter', was at a disadvantage in both search and use as neither the company nor the period was known. Context retrieval improves the input of both the embedding and BM25 by prefixing these chunks with a short description. This is why search quality must start from the context of chunks.

You can stack hybrid search and re-ranking on top of that. Embedding captures the meaning, BM25 captures the exact word, and reranking re-evaluates many candidates to leave only the top ones. In our measurements, this effect was cumulative. The default embedding's failure rate of 5.7% has been reduced to 1.9%.

However, the settings must be determined by evaluation. Chunk boundaries, number of chunks, and embedding models vary for each use case, and reranking increases delay and cost. Also remember that adding a general document summary has limited benefits. Each chunk needs a description that fits that chunk.

In practice, we can first create an evaluation question, inventory the failure rate of our chunks, add context explanation, hybridization, and re-ranking one by one, and compare the effectiveness and cost with the same evaluation.

callout.text: Even if you read the chunks in isolation, you should be able to tell which part of the document it is; if not, add context.

glossary.def: Information such as the company, time period, and location of the document the chunk belongs to. It's easy to lose documents when dividing them.
This is a technique for creating embeddings and BM25 indexes by prepending a context description to each chunk.
This is a method that uses an embedding search to capture meaning and a vocabulary search to find exact words.
This is the step where candidates collected through search are re-evaluated based on their relevance to the query, leaving only the top candidates.
A vocabulary-based function that ranks based on exact word or phrase matches.

misconceptions.myth: The smaller the chunk, the more accurate the search.
misconceptions.fact: The smaller you break it down, the more likely it is that each chunk will lose the context of the original document, resulting in more failures. Chunk boundaries and sizes must be determined by evaluation.

misconceptions.myth: Attaching a document summary to every chunk has the same effect.
misconceptions.fact: In Anthropic's experiment, adding generic document summaries had very limited benefits. Each chunk needs a context that describes that chunk.

misconceptions.myth: Re-ranking only increases quality at no additional cost.
misconceptions.fact: One more step at execution time, resulting in delays and costs. The balance between number of candidates and performance needs to be determined through experimentation in our use cases.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Search quality begins with chunks having self-contained context.
We improve both embedding and BM25 by attaching a context description to each chunk.
The benefits of hybrid search and reranking stack up, but at the cost of delays and costs.
Chunk boundaries and chunk numbers are determined by direct evaluation.
